summary: Proposes the Concise Data Definition Language, a notation for expressing CBOR data structures, and JSON structures as well. The goal is to describe protocol messages and data formats simply and unambiguously. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL) is a notation for describing which data structures a protocol allows. People can read its rules, and tools can use them to check CBOR or JSON data.

questions: what is concise data definition language
subtitle: A compact notation for describing the data structures allowed in CBOR and JSON.

tldr.problem: Protocols using CBOR need a clear, unambiguous way to describe their data structures so people can understand them and tools can check data against them.
tldr.mechanism: CDDL defines named rules using types and groups. Its notation describes arrays, maps, choices, optional or repeated entries, tags, and additional constraints called controls.
tldr.outcome: CDDL describes CBOR and can also describe JSON by restricting itself to values JSON can represent. RFC 8610 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9682.

today: RFC 8610 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9682; it has not been obsoleted. The RFC defines CDDL for describing CBOR structures and also permits its use with JSON.

sections.title: Why CDDL Was Defined
sections.content:
RFC 8610 defines the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL), a notation for describing Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures. Its goals include unambiguous descriptions, flexible representation choices, a readable format that machines can process, and support for checking data and extracting elements.

CDDL can also describe JSON because JSON's generic data model is a subset of CBOR's. That was a useful side effect rather than an original goal.
sections.plainLanguage: CDDL gives protocol designers a shared way to describe what valid data looks like. The same rules can guide people and support automatic checks.

sections.title: Types, Groups, and Choices
sections.content:
CDDL builds data descriptions from two main concepts: types and groups. A type says what values are allowed; a group is a list of entries that can be composed into an array or map. The first rule in a CDDL file defines the root type, which is the complete data structure described by the specification.

A slash (/) gives a choice between types, and a double slash (//) gives a choice between groups. A group can be named and reused to share common fields across structures. CDDL can also use CBOR representation types, including tags.
sections.plainLanguage: A type describes an allowed value, and a group describes a collection of entries. Rules combine these pieces, and choices let a value or group have more than one valid form.

sections.title: Rules, Occurrence, Arrays, and Maps
sections.content:
A CDDL rule gives a name to a type or group. Names are case-sensitive, comments begin with a semicolon, text strings use double quotes, and byte strings use single quotes. CDDL text is encoded using UTF-8.

Occurrence markers say whether an entry is optional or may repeat: the question-mark marker means zero or one, the asterisk marker means zero or more, and the plus marker means one or more. A bounded form can specify lower and upper limits. Without a marker, an entry occurs once.

Square brackets describe arrays, where order matters. Curly braces describe maps, where keys identify entries and order does not matter. CDDL can describe fixed-key structures and maps with a range of possible keys. The cut operator can prevent a key matched by one entry from matching a later entry.
sections.plainLanguage: CDDL uses short marks to say whether a field is required, optional, or repeatable. Arrays rely on position, while maps rely on keys and do not have a fixed order.

sections.title: Tags and Additional Constraints
sections.content:
A CDDL type can include a CBOR tag by writing the tag number and the type of the tagged value. The unwrap operator (~) exposes the group or inner type inside a named array, map, or tag, which lets a definition reuse those contents.

Control operators add constraints to a type. For example, .size limits a string's size, .bits limits which bits may be set, and .regexp requires a text string to match an XML Schema Definition regular expression. Other controls describe embedded CBOR, comparisons, or defaults.

The RFC defines 14 initial control operators and establishes an IANA registry for future operators. CDDL describes allowed data values; it does not prescribe whether arrays or maps use definite or indefinite-length encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Tags identify additional meaning for a value, and controls add conditions such as a size limit or a required pattern. These rules describe acceptable data, not every detail of how it must be encoded.

sections.title: Extension Points and Reusable Rules
sections.content:
CDDL defines extension points called sockets. A name beginning with $ is a type socket, and one beginning with $$ is a group socket. A socket starts empty; later rules can add choices with /= or //=, including rules kept in separate files.

It is not an error for a socket to remain undefined, in which case it provides no choices. By convention, definitions that add to a socket use the matching augmentation operator. Generic rules can also take parameters, allowing a type or group to be reused with different arguments.
sections.plainLanguage: A socket marks a place where a specification can add new choices later. Generic rules provide another way to reuse a definition with different values.

sections.title: Describing JSON Data
sections.content:
CDDL can describe JSON when the specification avoids byte strings, tags, and simple values other than false, true, and null. JSON has one number type, so CDDL's integer types test whether a JSON number is integral; a decimal point or exponent does not by itself make a value non-integral.

Applications that need I-JSON-compatible integers may define narrower ranges. RFC 8610 gives the interoperable integer range from -9007199254740991 through 9007199254740991. JSON cannot represent values such as NaN or infinity, even if a CDDL data model otherwise allows them.
sections.plainLanguage: The same notation can describe JSON if it uses only values JSON supports. A JSON number can match an integer rule when its value is integral, even if it is written with a decimal point or exponent.

sections.title: Using and Checking CDDL
sections.content:
CDDL can guide a human implementer, support automated checking of CBOR or JSON, and help data-analysis tools verify or extract information. Each application decides how strictly to enforce the description. The RFC says a CDDL tool is not intended to write implementation code.

CDDL itself does not introduce security issues, but protocols that use CBOR need their own security analysis. The RFC cautions against relying on a CDDL specification or matcher as the only defense, and says extension points need careful security consideration. It encourages clear, simple specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: CDDL can help people understand data and help software check it, but each application decides what to enforce. A protocol still needs its own security protections and analysis.
